questions.q: Starting from the centre of the earth having radius $R$, the variation of $g$ (acceleration due to gravity) is shown by
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity $g$ at a distance $r$ from the centre of the Earth is given by two different expressions depending on whether the point is inside or outside the Earth.

For $r < R$ (inside the Earth), assuming uniform density, the acceleration due to gravity is given by $g_{in} = \dfrac{GMr}{R^3}$. This shows that $g$ is directly proportional to $r$, i.e., $g \propto r$. The graph is a straight line passing through the origin with a positive slope.

For $r \ge R$ (outside the Earth), the acceleration due to gravity is given by $g_{out} = \dfrac{GM}{r^2}$. This shows that $g$ is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, i.e., $g \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}$. The graph is a curve that decreases as $r$ increases.

At the surface of the Earth ($r = R$), both expressions yield the same value $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$, which is the maximum value of $g$.

Combining these, the graph starts from the origin, increases linearly until $r = R$, and then decreases following an inverse-square law for $r > R$. This matches the fourth graph provided in the options.

questions.solution:
As the particles move& under gravitational influence, the gravitational force will provide the centripetal force required.&

Gravitational force between two bodies of masses& ${m}_{1} and {m}_{2}$ separated by distance $d$ is given by,~$G\dfrac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{d2}$, where~$G$~is the universal gravitational constant.

Net force on the particle& at $A$~due to& particles at $B$~and $C$~is,

$\overset{→}{F}net = \overset{→}{F}AC + \overset{→}{F}AB$

$\overset{→}{F}net = G\dfrac{M2}{L2}\overset{^}{AC} + G\dfrac{M2}{L2}\overset{^}{AB}$.

Here,~$\overset{^}{AB}$~and $\overset{^}{AC}$~are unit vectors along $AB and AC$.

On simplifying vector addition$\left(\text{taking}F = G\dfrac{M2}{L2}\right)$, we get,

${F}_{net} = 2Fcos\left(30 °\right) = 2G\dfrac{M2}{L2}\dfrac{3}{2} = \sqrt{3}G\dfrac{M2}{L2}$

From geometry, radius of circle,~$R = \dfrac{L}{3}$.

Since the~force ${F}_{net}$~provides the centripetal force required, so,

$⇒ \dfrac{Mv^{2}}{R} = \sqrt{3}G\dfrac{M2}{L2}$

$⇒ v^{2} = \sqrt{3}G\dfrac{MR}{L2} = \sqrt{3}G\dfrac{M\left(\dfrac{L}{\sqrt{3}}\right)}{L2} = \dfrac{GM}{L}$

$⇒ v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{L}}$.

$\left[$\text{as}$\left(1 + $\dfrac{h ⁡}{R ⁡}\right)$-2 ⋍ 1 - $\dfrac{2h ⁡}{R ⁡}$\right]$

So substituting the given data,

$T ⁡ = \dfrac{3 \times 100 \times 10 \times 64}{6400 \times {10}^{3}} =3 \times {10}^{- 2}$\text{N}$

When the point mass nearer to $M$ is at a distance $r = 3l$ from $M$, the tension in the rod is zero for $m = k \left(\dfrac{M}{288}\right). The value of $k$ is

$
questions.solution:
Due to gravitational interaction connected masses have some acceleration.

Let both small masses are moving with acceleration 'a' towards larger mass M



Force equation for mass nearer to a larger mass

$\dfrac{GMm}{\left(3l\right)2} - \dfrac{Gm^{2}}{l2} = ma$ ...(i)

Force equation for mass away from a larger mass

$\dfrac{GMm}{\left(4l\right)2} + \dfrac{Gm^{2}}{l2} = ma$ ...(ii)

From equation (i) & (ii)

$\dfrac{GM}{9l^{2}} - \dfrac{Gm}{l2} = \dfrac{GM}{16l^{2}} + \dfrac{Gm}{l2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{M}{9} - \dfrac{M}{16} = m + m$

$\dfrac{7M}{144} = 2m$

$⇒ m = \dfrac{7M}{288} = k \left(\dfrac{M}{288}\right)

$⇒ k = 7$

If we assume that there is a hypothetical planet which moves around the sun in a circular orbit of radius ${r}_{0} = \dfrac{r + R}{2}$, then the time period of this hypothetical planet and our given planet will be same. The time period of a planet around the sun in circular orbit is
